section.title: Zophar's First Speech
section.sectionRationale: Zophar is the harshest of the three friends from his very first words, accusing Job of babbling and even suggesting, in the sharpest line any friend has yet spoken, that God is actually exacting less punishment from Job than his sin deserves. He appeals to the unsearchable depths of God's wisdom, an argument that is entirely true, and then uses it to imply Job's suffering is a mystery Job has no right to question.
section.thesis: Zophar rightly insists that God's wisdom is unfathomably deep, but wrongly weaponizes that truth to imply Job's suffering must be deserved and that only repentance for hidden sin can restore him, closing the first cycle of speeches on its harshest note yet.
section.frameNote: Four movements: Zophar's blunt accusation that Job's stream of words deserves rebuke, and his sharp claim that God exacts from Job less than his iniquity deserves; his appeal to the unsearchable depths of divine wisdom, higher than the heavens and deeper than Sheol; his conditional promise that Job's misery will end if he puts away iniquity; and his closing warning that the eyes of the wicked will fail with no escape.

units.label: Should such a speaker be vindicated?
units.note: God exacts less than your iniquity deserves

verses.text: Then Zophar the Naamathite replied:
"Should this stream of words go unanswered and such a speaker be vindicated?
Should your babbling put others to silence? Will you scoff without rebuke?
You have said, 'My doctrine is sound, and I am pure in Your sight.'
But if only God would speak and open His lips against you,
and disclose to you the {{taalumah|secrets}} of wisdom, for true wisdom has two sides. Know then that God exacts from you less than your iniquity deserves.

units.label: Can you fathom the deep things of God?
units.note: higher than the heavens, deeper than Sheol

verses.text: "Can you fathom the deep things of God or discover the limits of the Almighty?
They are higher than the heavens: what can you do? They are deeper than Sheol: what can you know?
Their measure is longer than the earth and wider than the sea.
If He comes along to imprison you, or convenes a court, who can stop Him?
Surely He knows the deceit of men. If He sees iniquity, does He not take note?
But a {{nabub|witless}} man can no more become wise than the colt of a wild donkey can be born a man!

units.label: If you direct your heart to Him
units.note: your life will be brighter than noonday

verses.text: "As for you, if you direct your heart and lift up your hands to Him,
if you put away the iniquity in your hand, and allow no injustice to dwell in your tents,
then indeed you will lift up your face without shame; you will stand firm and unafraid.
For you will forget your misery, recalling it only as waters gone by.
Your life will be brighter than noonday; its darkness will be like the morning.
You will be secure, because there is {{tiqvah|hope}}, and you will look around and lie down in safety.
You will lie down without fear, and many will court your favor.

units.label: The eyes of the wicked will fail
units.note: they will hope for their last breath

verses.text:
But the eyes of the wicked will fail, and escape will elude them; 
they will hope for their last {{nephesh|breath}}."

taalumah.gloss: A secret, hidden thing, mystery. Zophar claims that if God revealed the secrets of His wisdom to Job, it would show God is actually treating Job more leniently than he deserves; the claim assumes exactly the guilt the reader knows Job does not bear.

nabub.gloss: Hollow, empty-headed, witless. Zophar uses it to insult Job's capacity for wisdom, comparing him to a wild donkey's colt that could sooner be born human than a fool become wise, one of the harshest personal jabs any friend levels at Job in the whole book.

tiqvah.gloss: Hope, expectation, something to look forward to. Zophar promises that repentance will restore Job's hope and security; the tragedy is that Job already has integrity, so the repentance Zophar demands cannot be the actual path to restoration his case requires.

nephesh.gloss: Soul, life, breath, the animating self of a person. Zophar's closing image of the wicked hoping for their last breath, their nephesh's final expiring, portrays a bleak end with no escape, a warning aimed at Job that, by the book's own frame, is misdirected at an innocent man.

basic.context: Zophar, the last and harshest of the three friends to speak in this first cycle, wastes no time with gentleness. He accuses Job of babbling and claims that if God actually revealed His hidden wisdom, it would show that Job's punishment is lighter than his sin deserves, a stunning claim given what the reader already knows about Job's innocence. He grounds his argument in the genuinely true fact that God's wisdom is unsearchably deep, higher than the heavens and deeper than Sheol, then promises that if Job will put away his iniquity, his life will become brighter than noonday. He closes with a bleak warning about the fate of the wicked, whose eyes fail and who have nothing left to hope for but their last breath.
basic.hermeneutics: Zophar's theology of divine mystery is entirely correct, God's wisdom truly is beyond human fathoming, but his application is the cruelest of the three friends: he assumes this unsearchable wisdom justifies concluding that Job deserves even worse than he has received. The chapter shows that appeals to mystery, however true, can be misused just as easily as appeals to tradition or private vision when wielded to accuse rather than to humble.
basic.originalLanguages: Zophar claims that God's ta'alumah, hidden wisdom, would prove Job deserves more punishment, not less, and calls Job nabub, hollow or witless, one of the sharpest personal insults in the book. He promises restored tiqvah, hope, if Job repents, and closes with a bleak image of the wicked whose nephesh, breath or soul, gives out with nothing left to hope for.
basic.typology: Zophar's claim that God's wisdom is higher than the heavens and deeper than Sheol anticipates the fuller unveiling of that same unsearchable wisdom in Christ, in whom, as Paul says, all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden, made known not to accuse the innocent but to save the guilty.
basic.christ: Zophar rightly says no one can fathom the deep things of God, yet this same unsearchable God has made Himself known in Christ, in whom the mystery of God's wisdom is finally disclosed, not to condemn an innocent sufferer further but to bear condemnation on behalf of the truly guilty. Where Zophar's mystery is used to silence Job's protest, the gospel's mystery, once hidden and now revealed, is used to comfort and save.
basic.god: God's wisdom is real and vast beyond human reach, exactly as Zophar says; the problem is not Zophar's doctrine of God but his confidence that this unsearchable wisdom can be used as a weapon to conclude Job's guilt. The chapter warns that mystery cited to silence a sufferer's honest questions is mystery misused.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 11:33-34 marvels at the depth of God's wisdom and knowledge, unsearchable, using language remarkably close to Zophar's; Colossians 2:3 locates all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge in Christ; Isaiah 55:8-9 affirms God's ways are higher than human ways, though there used to comfort rather than accuse.
basic.oneStory: Zophar's true doctrine of divine mystery, wielded as an accusation against an innocent man, closes the first cycle of speeches on its harshest note. The book will let this very truth, God's unsearchable wisdom, return properly at its climax, when God speaks from the whirlwind, not to accuse Job of secret sin but to humble him with wonder, and it points forward to the wisdom finally and savingly revealed in Christ.

context.literary:
Zophar's speech is twenty verses, the shortest so far, and it is the closing panel of the first round of the debate. It has the shape of a prosecutor's speech: the charge in verses 2 to 4, a wish that the judge would speak in verses 5 and 6, an argument from the size of God in verses 7 to 12, an offer of terms in verses 13 to 19, and a warning in verse 20. The two ends of the speech are joined by the theme of what God knows. In verse 6 God would disclose the secrets of wisdom, and in verse 11 He knows the deceit of men, so that the judge who cannot be fathomed is the judge who cannot be fooled.

The central section is a small poem in four dimensions. Verses 8 and 9 measure the thing they are describing upward as higher than the heavens, downward as deeper than Sheol, lengthwise as longer than the earth, and across as wider than the sea. The directions are given in the order that will later become a formula, and the effect is to say that there is no direction in which the edge of God can be found. Verse 10 then swings the reader back from geometry to law, and asks who could stop God if He arrested and convened a court.

The offer of verses 13 to 19 is built on a chain of conditionals. If you direct your heart, if you put away iniquity, then you will lift up your face, forget misery, and lie down in safety. Each of the results is a reversal of something Job has said. He has said that his days flee without seeing good, Job 9:25, and Zophar promises a life brighter than noonday. He has said he is full of shame, Job 10:15, and Zophar promises a face lifted without shame. The speech is a designed answer to the last two chapters.

The final verse closes on the eyes of the wicked failing, and it echoes the hope that Zophar has just promised, so that the last word is a fork. There is a tiqvah for the one who repents and none for the one who does not.
context.historical:
Zophar the Naamathite is the third of the friends, and of the three he is the least identifiable. The place from which he takes his name is not certainly known, and the book does not fix it. What matters historically is the kind of speaker he is. In the ancient East, when a man's fortunes collapsed, it was normal for friends and neighbours to come and offer a diagnosis, and the diagnosis was nearly always moral. The gods, or God, had been offended; the sufferer had to find how. A sufferer who insisted he was innocent was a difficulty, because he threatened the framework in which everyone understood the world.

Zophar's language of seeking and fathoming has a home in the wisdom schools of the region. The wise were those who searched things out, and Job 28 will later say that man mines the earth for silver and gold but cannot find the place of wisdom. Zophar's sarcasm that a witless man can no more become wise than a wild donkey's colt can be born a man draws on ordinary knowledge of the wild ass, a creature that in Israel's poetry stood for untamed freedom, Job 39:5-8. His picture of the hands stretched out in prayer in verse 13 belongs to the normal posture of prayer in Israel, seen also in Psalm 28:2. And his promise that many will court your favor, verse 19, reflects a society in which a household's standing depended on public honour, so that restoration meant a return of one's reputation as much as one's health.

The legal frame is also historical. When Zophar speaks of God imprisoning, or convening a court, verse 10, he uses the vocabulary of a judge who can seize a person, hold him and hear his case in an assembly, and the friends assume that such a court would find Job guilty.
context.canonical:
The measuring of God in verses 7 to 9 echoes through the rest of Scripture. David confesses that knowledge of God is too wonderful for him and too lofty to attain, and that even in Sheol God is there, Psalm 139:6-8. Isaiah records the LORD saying that His thoughts are higher than ours, Isaiah 55:8-9. Paul comes to the end of his great argument in Romans with the cry, O, the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God, how unsearchable are His judgments, and untraceable His ways, Romans 11:33. In Ephesians he prays that the readers will grasp the length and width and height and depth of the love of Christ, Ephesians 3:18-19, borrowing the same four dimensions Zophar used for God's wisdom and giving them to a love that surpasses knowledge.

Zophar's theology of secrets is also a scriptural one. Moses tells Israel that the secret things belong to the LORD but the things revealed belong to us, Deuteronomy 29:29. The difference is that Moses draws a line to encourage obedience, while Zophar uses the line to close Job's mouth. The same doctrine can serve humility or accusation, and the book of Job is one long lesson in the difference.

His suggestion that God exacts less than iniquity deserves has parallels in the prayers of Israel. Ezra says that God has punished us less than our iniquities deserve, Ezra 9:13, and the psalmist says God has not dealt with us according to our sins, Psalm 103:10. Both speak in confession, in the first person plural. Zophar says it in the second person to a man who has not confessed anything. And the promise that darkness will be like the morning finds a parallel in Isaiah 58:10, where the night becomes like noonday for the one who gives himself to the hungry.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The poet uses Zophar to show the last and most dangerous form of the friends' mistake. Eliphaz appealed to an experience and Bildad to tradition, and both had a source outside themselves. Zophar appeals to a doctrine that is true, the greatness of God, and uses it as a weapon. The reader is meant to feel that the most orthodox voice in the room is also the one who has left the least room for the sufferer.

The author also wants us to see how a speaker can fail to listen. Zophar says that Job has claimed his doctrine is sound and that he is pure in God's sight. Job has said nothing so tidy. He has said that he is blameless, Job 9:21, and that he has not denied the words of the Holy One, Job 6:10, but the phrase Zophar quotes is his own compression. This is how debates go wrong. The friend answers a caricature, and the sufferer is invited to defend a position he never took.

And the poet builds in a long irony. Zophar wishes that God would speak and open His lips against Job, verse 5. God does speak, in chapter 38, and He speaks against no one but the friends' picture of Him. The first hearers, who had the ending, would have enjoyed the reversal, and would have learned that a wish for God to condemn a fellow sufferer is a dangerous thing to wish aloud.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records a speech that God will later call inaccurate, and so we cannot lift its conclusions into a rule. Zophar's demand that Job repent of a hidden sin as a condition of restoration is not what Scripture teaches about suffering as such. The book of Job is written in part to deny that inference. Yet some of what he says is sound and can be taken up as teaching: God is beyond our full understanding, verses 7 to 9; He sees iniquity and takes note, verse 11; a person who turns to Him with the whole heart and puts away wrong can hope, verses 13 to 15; and those who reject Him have no lasting refuge, verse 20.

The right use is to sort them. Where Scripture elsewhere confirms these points, as in Psalm 139:6 and Psalm 32:5, we can accept them. Where Zophar applies them to Job's case, we should hear the correction that God delivers in chapter 42. The passage gives a warning to anyone tempted to use the greatness of God as a reason to press a burdened person for a confession that they may not have to make.

debates.question: What does Zophar say God does with Job's iniquity in verse 6?

views.label: God exacts less than it deserves
views.case: This is the BSB's rendering, and it fits the sense of Ezra 9:13 and Psalm 103:10, where God's judgment is milder than our guilt deserves. Zophar means it as an accusation: Job is being let off lightly and should be grateful.

views.label: God has let some of Job's iniquity be forgotten
views.case: Some translators take the verb as a form meaning to forget, so that God has overlooked part of Job's guilt. The sense is similar: Job has not received the full sentence he has earned. In both readings the meaning for the argument is the same, that his suffering is smaller than his sin.

debates.bearing: The translation changes the phrasing more than the point. Either way Zophar treats mercy as a reason for Job to stop protesting, which turns a truth about grace into a tool of pressure.

debates.question: Is an appeal to the mystery of God a good answer to a sufferer?

views.label: Yes, mystery is the truest answer
views.case: God does say in the end that Job cannot comprehend His ways, and Deuteronomy 29:29 draws the line between the secret things and revealed things. A sufferer who insists on a complete explanation demands what no creature can have.

views.label: Only if the speaker also admits he does not know
views.case: Zophar claims to be able to say that Job deserves worse, which is knowledge about the very secrets he says no one can fathom. Mystery invoked by someone who then explains everything is not humility, it is a way of ending the conversation.

debates.bearing: The book itself takes the second view. God's speeches later point to the same unfathomable depths, but they do so to bring Job to worship and not to condemn him, and the difference between the two uses is the test of whether a comforter has understood what mystery means.

study.originalLanguages:
Zophar begins with a name for Job that is easy to miss. In verse 2 the man who is asked to be vindicated is, in the Hebrew, a man of lips. A man of lips is someone whose worth is all in his talk. The word for justified, tsadaq, is the same root as righteous, so that the question is a legal one: should such a man be declared in the right? Zophar assumes the answer is no before he starts.

In verse 3 the babbling is a single Hebrew word for empty talk, and the verb for scoffing is the one used elsewhere of mockery, so that he accuses Job of both nonsense and contempt. The accusation matters because Job's words in chapter 9 had not been contemptuous of God's greatness, only anguished about His justice. The verbal gap between what Job said and what Zophar heard is where the conversation breaks.

The phrase in verse 6 that BSB renders true wisdom has two sides is literally something like the double of sound wisdom. The Hebrew word for double points to something folded over, twice as much, and the idea seems to be that the wisdom of God has a hidden side beyond the visible one. Zophar uses this to claim that there is more to Job's case than Job can see and that the extra will tell against him. That is an odd move for a man who cannot see it either.

The secrets of wisdom in verse 6 are things hidden, the same family of words used for the secrets of the heart in Psalm 44:21. It is the language of what only God can bring to light. Zophar wants God to reveal what is hidden about Job. The book of Job will let God reveal what is hidden, but it will be the hiddenness of the world and not of Job's heart.

In verse 7 the two verbs, to fathom and to discover the limit, are both verbs of exploration, and the object of the second is the limit of the Almighty, a word for the end or perfection of a thing. He is asking Job whether he can find the boundary of God, and the reader of the New Testament hears the reply in Ephesians 3:18-19, where the dimensions of Christ's love exceed knowledge.

Verse 12 has a footnote that deserves notice: the wild donkey's colt can no more be born a man, or, as the footnote says, can be born tame. Both readings are possible in the Hebrew, and both make the same point, that a fool changes as little as a wild ass changes. The insult is that Job is beyond teaching.

Finally, in verse 20 the last breath is literally an exhaling of the soul, and the word nephesh is here the life itself. The wicked hope for nothing but the moment their life goes out. It is a stark end to a speech that began with a promise, and the abruptness is deliberate.

typology.fulfillment: Zophar's picture of the wisdom of God as deeper than Sheol, a place no one can fathom, finds a striking sequel in the person who went there. Psalm 139:8 says that if I make my bed in Sheol, You are there, and Ephesians 4:9-10 says that Christ descended to the lower parts of the earth and ascended above all the heavens, to fill all things. The two ends of Zophar's measurement, the heights of heaven and the depths of Sheol, are both traversed by the Son. The type falls short because Zophar sets the depth out of reach of any human, while the New Testament says it has been reached by God in human flesh, and that he has come back.

typology.type: The lifted face without shame, Job 11:15
typology.fulfillment: Zophar promises that Job will lift up his face without shame if he puts away wrong. The New Testament promises the same result on a different ground. Anyone who believes in Him will never be put to shame, Romans 10:11, because Christ endured the cross and despised its shame, Hebrews 12:2, and took the guilt that produces shame. The escalation is from a shame lifted by our effort to a shame borne by another. The type falls short because Zophar's condition makes the lifting depend on Job's repentance, while the gospel makes it depend on Christ's finished work, received by faith.

The promise that Job's life will be brighter than noonday, and its darkness like the morning, points to the coming of the true light. Jesus says, I am the light of the world, whoever follows Me will never walk in darkness, John 8:12, and Malachi had promised that the sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its wings, Malachi 4:2. At the last there will be no more night, Revelation 22:5. The type falls short because Zophar's light is a reward for a good life, and in Christ the light is a gift that comes into the dark and lights those who had no claim on it.

study.christ:
Zophar's speech leads to Christ first through the theme of hidden wisdom. His demand that God should disclose the secrets of wisdom, verse 6, and his insistence that no one can fathom the deep things of God, verse 7, are met by Paul's astonishing claim that in Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, Colossians 2:3. The secret that Zophar thought could not be reached has a face. Paul says that the hidden wisdom of God, destined for our glory before time began, has been revealed to us by the Spirit, who searches even the deep things of God, 1 Corinthians 2:7-10. What Zophar treats as a wall is, in the gospel, a door.

The second link is his claim that God exacts less than iniquity deserves. That is true in a way Zophar did not know, and the truth is expensive. God does not deal with us as our sins deserve, Psalm 103:10, because the deserved penalty has been placed on someone else. Paul says that God passed over former sins in His forbearance, and that He did so in order to show His justice in the present time, so that He might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus, Romans 3:25-26. Zophar's line becomes the gospel when we ask why the sentence is lighter than the guilt. It is lighter for us because it was heavier for Him.

A third link is the contrast between the friend's use of mystery and the way Christ speaks about it. Zophar uses depth to silence. Jesus uses it to invite. He thanks the Father that He has hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to little children, Matthew 11:25, and He says that all who are weary and burdened may come to Him, Matthew 11:28. The God who cannot be fathomed comes down in a person who says, Come. Zophar cannot imagine that.

The promise at the end of the offer, that Job will forget his misery like waters gone by, has a fulfilment in the promise that God will wipe away every tear, Revelation 21:4, and, in the wording of the new covenant, that He will remember sins no more, Hebrews 8:12. Zophar promises forgetting as a reward for a clean record. The gospel promises it to the unclean who are washed.

The passage also invites a caution. Job is not Christ and Zophar is not the devil. To say that a sufferer in the book of Job is a picture of the Lord would pull the book out of shape. It is enough to see that where Zophar's argument fails, Christ's work supplies what was missing, and that the God whom Zophar could only measure is the God who came near enough to be touched.
study.god:
The most important sentence in Zophar's speech about God is the one that is most easily quoted alone: Can you fathom the deep things of God or discover the limits of the Almighty? The answer is no, and the answer is a true one. The doctrine of divine incomprehensibility, that no creature can exhaust God, is written into Scripture from Deuteronomy 29:29 to Romans 11:33. It does not mean that we know nothing of God. It means that what we know is real and never complete, and that His wisdom always exceeds our grasp. Worship begins there.

The second thing the speech says is that God knows everything about human hearts, verse 11. He knows the deceit of men, and if He sees iniquity, He takes note. That is the doctrine of omniscience as it bears on responsibility, and it is repeated in the Psalms, where nothing is hidden from Him, Psalm 139:1-4. The knowledge that terrifies Zophar's hearer is also the knowledge that can be a comfort, since the God who sees the guilty also sees the innocent, and the book of Job says explicitly that He has already declared Job blameless, Job 1:8 and 2:3.

The third is the irony of the wish in verse 5. Zophar says, If only God would speak and open His lips against you. This tells us how the friends think of God: as one who has only a verdict to deliver. When God does speak, in Job 38:1-3, He does not deliver the verdict Zophar expects. He speaks of the world, of creatures and seasons, and then He speaks to the friends and not to Job, saying that they have not spoken accurately of Him. So the God of this chapter is a God who chooses the time and the terms of His speaking, and who is not at the disposal of anyone's arguments.

The fourth concerns His mercy. Zophar says, in a hard way, that God gives less than iniquity deserves. The Bible agrees that God is slow to anger and abounding in love, Psalm 103:8-10, and that His mercy is the reason any of us are here. The lesson is that God's mercy is the ground of the sinner's hope, not a reproach to the sufferer. What Zophar misuses as an accusation is what the psalmist sings as a gift.

For worship, this speech teaches us to hold high truths about God with low hands. We can say that God is beyond us, that He knows all, and that He is merciful, and we should say them as those who need each of them. We should say them first of ourselves. To say them primarily of another person's guilt is to have misunderstood what they are for.

crossReferences.note: David says that such knowledge is too wonderful for him and that if he made his bed in Sheol, God would be there. It shares Zophar's language of heights and depths, but the psalmist takes the greatness of God as a comfort that reaches even the grave, where Zophar takes it as a reason for Job to be silent.

Paul closes his long argument about God's purposes with a cry over the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God, whose judgments are unsearchable. It stands in the line of Job 11:7. Paul shows that the right response to God's unfathomable depth is praise, not a demand that a suffering person concede guilt.

Paul prays that believers may grasp the length, width, height and depth of the love of Christ, which surpasses knowledge. The four dimensions echo Zophar's measure of God in Job 11:8-9. What Zophar gives to the mystery of wisdom, Paul gives to a love that has been made known.

In Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, and the mystery of God is Christ Himself. Zophar's secrets of wisdom become a person. This passage answers the demand of Job 11:5-6 for God to disclose what is hidden.

The secret things belong to the LORD, but the things revealed belong to us. It gives the sound version of Zophar's principle. The limit on our knowledge is meant to drive us to obey what has been shown, not to justify a verdict about someone else's hidden guilt.

Ezra confesses that God has punished the people less than their iniquities deserve. It shares the sentiment of Job 11:6, but in the mouth of one who is confessing his own sin along with his nation's. That is the difference between a prayer and a charge.

He has not dealt with us according to our sins or repaid us according to our iniquities. The psalmist sings the truth Zophar states with a sneer. The same fact, that God gives less than we deserve, produces worship in David and accusation in Zophar.

For those who give themselves to the hungry, the night becomes like noonday. The image matches Job 11:17, and shows that the promise of dawn out of darkness belongs to those who turn to care for others. It reminds us that the friends' promise has a real biblical shape, even though it was misapplied to Job.

The LORD answers Job out of the whirlwind. Zophar wished that God would speak against Job; God speaks and asks Job to brace himself like a man. It is the fulfilment of the wish of 11:5, though not in the way Zophar meant, and it moves the book from accusation to encounter.

Paul speaks of the mysterious and hidden wisdom of God, revealed to us by the Spirit, who searches even the deep things of God. It reverses Zophar's question, Can you fathom the deep things of God. The answer is that by ourselves we cannot, but God has made them known.

study.oneStory:
Zophar's picture of a God too high to be measured and too wise to be fooled belongs to the deepest layer of the Bible's story, the difference between the Creator and the creature. In Genesis 1 and 2, the man and woman walk with a God they know but do not master. The fall begins when the serpent suggests that they could be like God, knowing good and evil, Genesis 3:5, and so hide the limit that made them creatures. Zophar has the right instinct that the limit matters, and no one in the book of Job denies him that.

What he lacks is the sense that God has spoken in order to be known. Deuteronomy 29:29 sets the secret things beside the revealed things, and the story of redemption is the story of the revealed things multiplying: a name at the bush, a law from the mountain, prophets who say Thus says the LORD, and then a Son. The wisdom literature of Israel praises the wisdom that was with God at creation, Proverbs 8:22-31, and the New Testament identifies it with Christ, 1 Corinthians 1:24, who is the wisdom of God.

The promise that Zophar attaches to repentance, a life brighter than noonday, security and the end of fear, is a shadow of the promises the prophets make to the whole people of God. Isaiah speaks of light that will rise upon Zion, and Jeremiah speaks of a hope and a future, Jeremiah 29:11. These promises are given to a people who have been exiled for their sin, and given on the ground of the LORD's own mercy, not as a bargain. The story of Israel is Zophar's speech turned inside out: the people did not put away their iniquity first, and yet God restored them.

The story ends where Zophar's speech points and does not reach. In the new creation the depths that no one could fathom are not closed but opened, and the redeemed know as they are known, 1 Corinthians 13:12. There is no night, and no tears, and no death, Revelation 21:4 and 22:5. The tiqvah that Zophar dangled before Job becomes the hope that does not put us to shame, Romans 5:5, and the last word is not the failing of the eyes of the wicked but the sight of the face of God, Revelation 22:4.

quiz.q: What is the most striking accusation Zophar makes against Job in 11:6?

options.text: That God is actually exacting from Job less punishment than his iniquity deserves.
options.note: This is arguably the harshest single claim made by any friend in the book, directly contradicted by God's own earlier testimony about Job's blamelessness.

options.text: That God's hidden wisdom would reveal Job to be guiltier than his suffering has so far shown.
options.note: A close restatement of Zophar's claim, though less blunt than his own direct wording about deserved punishment.

options.text: That God has no knowledge of Job's situation.
options.note: Zophar's argument assumes God's full knowledge and active judgment, not divine ignorance.

options.text: That Job has never actually suffered at all.
options.note: Zophar does not deny Job's suffering; he claims it is insufficient given Job's supposed guilt.

quiz.q: What true doctrine does Zophar affirm about God's wisdom in 11:7-9?

options.text: That it is unsearchably deep, higher than the heavens and deeper than Sheol, beyond any human ability to fathom.
options.note: This claim is doctrinally sound and echoed elsewhere in Scripture, such as Romans 11:33-36 and Isaiah 55:8-9.

options.text: That its measure is longer than the earth and wider than the sea, far beyond what any person could hope to trace out.
options.note: A true restatement of Zophar's own imagery in verse 9, though less complete than the fuller heavens-and-Sheol picture in verse 8.

options.text: That human wisdom and divine wisdom are essentially equal.
options.note: Zophar's argument specifically denies this, insisting on a vast gap between human and divine wisdom.

options.text: That God's wisdom can be fully understood by careful study.
options.note: Zophar's point is the opposite: God's wisdom exceeds human capacity to fully grasp it.

quiz.q: What condition does Zophar attach to his promise of restored hope for Job (11:13-19)?

options.text: That Job direct his heart to God, put away iniquity from his hand, and allow no injustice to remain in his household.
options.note: Zophar's promise is entirely conditional on repentance for sin the reader already knows Job has not committed in the way Zophar assumes.

options.text: That Job turn his heart back to God and clear his household of any lingering injustice.
options.note: A close paraphrase of Zophar's actual condition, though slightly less complete than his full listing of both inner and outward repentance.

options.text: That Job offer a specific sacrifice at the temple.
options.note: No temple sacrifice is specified here; Zophar's condition is about inner repentance and just conduct, not ritual observance.

options.text: That Job simply wait patiently without any action required.
options.note: Zophar's promise is explicitly conditional on Job's active repentance, not passive waiting.

quiz.q: How does the book's own frame expose the flaw in Zophar's argument?

options.text: The reader already knows from chapters 1 and 2 that Job's suffering was not caused by sin, so Zophar's confident claim of hidden guilt is contradicted by information Zophar himself does not have.
options.note: This dramatic irony, information the reader has that the characters lack, is central to how the book exposes each friend's argument in turn.

options.text: Zophar's confidence outruns what he could actually know, since he was never present at the heavenly council described in chapters 1 and 2.
options.note: Correctly points toward the dramatic irony at work, though less precise than stating plainly what the reader already knows and Zophar does not.

options.text: The book shows that Zophar was lying deliberately to hurt Job.
options.note: The text gives no indication of deliberate deception; Zophar appears to sincerely believe his own theological framework.

options.text: God directly interrupts Zophar's speech to correct him on the spot.
options.note: God does not speak until much later in the book, in chapters 38 to 41; there is no immediate divine interruption here.

quiz.q: What is the ultimate biblical answer to the truth Zophar states about God's unsearchable wisdom?

options.text: Christ, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden and made known, not to accuse the innocent but to save the guilty.
options.note: Colossians 2:3 presents Christ as the fulfillment of the unsearchable wisdom Zophar rightly describes but wrongly applies.

options.text: Paul's own doxology on the unsearchable judgments and untraceable paths of God in Romans 11.
options.note: A true and closely related answer, though less complete than naming Christ Himself as the fuller revelation of that same wisdom.

options.text: There is no further biblical development of this theme beyond Job.
options.note: Romans 11:33-36 and Colossians 2:3 both develop this exact theme significantly beyond what Zophar states here.

options.text: The eventual scientific discovery of all God's hidden purposes.
options.note: Scripture consistently presents God's deepest purposes as revealed through Christ, not through human scientific advancement.

questions: Zophar's claim that God's wisdom is unsearchable is entirely true, yet he uses it to accuse rather than to humble himself. Where have you used a true belief about God to win an argument rather than to grow in humility?

Zophar tells a grieving, afflicted man that he is actually receiving less punishment than he deserves. Have you ever received, or given, comfort that technically sounded theological but actually wounded rather than healed?

Zophar's promise of restoration depends entirely on Job's repentance for a sin he has not committed in the way assumed. Where might you be waiting for your own life to improve based on a condition God has not actually set?

The true doctrine of God's unsearchable wisdom returns later in the book, spoken rightly by God Himself to humble Job with wonder rather than accusation. What is the difference between citing a truth about God to shut down someone's questions and using it to invite them into wonder?

Zophar is the harshest of the three friends, yet the book never portrays him as insincere. How do you guard your own certainty about someone else's situation, even when you believe you are speaking sound theology?

translationNotes.note: Secrets renders ta'alumah, hidden or mysterious things; Zophar's claim that these secrets would prove Job's guilt is an inference the text nowhere supports and the narrator's frame in chapters 1 and 2 directly contradicts.
Higher than the heavens, deeper than Sheol uses merism, pairing extreme opposites to express totality, a common Hebrew poetic device conveying that God's wisdom spans every possible dimension.

Witless renders nabub, literally hollow, and the comparison to a wild donkey's colt being born human is a proverbial way of saying something is essentially impossible, one of the sharpest insults leveled at Job in the book.
